articles.title: China Miéville’s The Rouse Is a Haunting Magnum Opus
articles.author: Jon Repetti
articles.content_excerpt: China Miéville’s The Rouse is a book that should not exist, and yet here it is. It should be read cover to cover, and then immediately read a second time. For twenty-one years, Miéville wrote and rewrote it while publishing shorter works at an impressive pace: four novels; two novellas; a history of the Russian Revolution; a book-length essay on The Communist Manifesto ; an out-of-left-field collaboration with Keanu Reeves; a children’s book with Zak Smith; countless articles and reviews. Each of these now seems like a stepping stone on Miéville’s path toward his great project. Into The Rouse ’s 1,200-plus pages have gone a lifetime of writing as well as a lifetime of reading — Miéville’s influences range from pulp horror to high modernism, from Marxist theory to esoterica. articles.author: Peter Cole
articles.content_excerpt: In 1984, while the global struggle against apartheid burned hot, union dockworkers in San Francisco refused to unload South African cargo to demonstrate their hostility to a white supremacist, fascist regime. In so doing they reaffirmed what Harry Bridges, the first president of the International Longshore and Warehouse Union (ILWU), asserted when asked about what role organized workers should play in world affairs: “Interfere with the foreign policy of the country? Sure as hell! That’s our job, that’s our privilege, that’s our right, that’s our duty.” Few workers believe that they have sufficient power to express political opinions at work, let alone insert themselves into global affairs by downing their tools. articles.content_excerpt: Jewish and Arab voters with Israeli citizenship massively flocked to voting stations on Tuesday, October 27, for the elections to the Israeli parliament, the Knesset. These were the first elections since the formation, in 2022, of the most reactionary government in the Zionist state’s history. articles.title: France’s Protests Fuel a Wider Fight Over Europe’s Future
articles.author: Harrison Stetler
articles.content_excerpt: The social unrest currently gripping France is in many ways a national phenomenon. Frustration with a stretched education system boiled over in the form of campus blockages and marches beginning late last month. By mid-October, students were joined by broader swaths of the population fed up with high gasoline prices, sticky inflation, and declining real wages. There’s also little new in the violent police response that has shocked protesters and observers alike, both in France and abroad. Emmanuel Macron’s allies above all want to protect the president’s agenda of pro-business tax cuts, an often-elided factor in the country’s fiscal crisis. articles.author: Rochester Red Star: News from Rochester DSA
articles.content_excerpt: Eugene V. Debs Eugene V. Debs (1855 – 1926) was a union leader and socialist politician. As presidential candidate for the Socialist Party of America, Debs received 6% of the popular vote in 1912. In June of 1918, Debs was arrested for a speech that urged resistance to the military draft in violation of the Espionage Act. He delivered the following statement to the court at his sentencing to ten years imprisonment. Debs ran for president from prison in 1920, receiving 3.4% of the vote. President Warren G. Harding commuted his sentence on December 23, 1921. articles.content_excerpt: The Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) is entering a new phase. Now, as chapters across the country call for Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez to run for president in 2028, the organization faces a crucial test of how to turn its growing popularity into national political power. There are encouraging signs that DSA is rising to the occasion. From Los Angeles and Chicago to smaller communities like Ithaca and Wichita, chapters have passed resolutions urging AOC to run. articles.title: Lula Defeats Bolsonaro - YDSA
articles.content_excerpt: Incumbent Victory Rolls Back Latin America’s Right Wing Wave Incumbent President Luiz Inácio “Lula” da Silva came ahead in the second round of Brazil’s Presidential election, winning a fourth term for the left-wing Worker’s Party (PT) candidate. The results are 51% for Lula, and 48% for Flavio Bolsonaro , candidate for the Liberal Party (PL) and son of former president Jair Bolsonaro, who is currently serving a 27-year sentence for plotting a coup after losing the 2022 election to Lula. Sunday’s victory is a significant comeback for Lula. When the first round of voting ended on October 4, Bolsonaro was ahead, 47% to Lula’s 45%.
